Photograph: NASA/Interim Archives/Getty Andrew Lynch Sat Aug 15 2026 - 04:47 • 2 MIN READ Stealing Hitler’s Rocket Author : Guy Walters ISBN-13 : 978-1035910854 Publisher : Head of Zeus Guideline Price : £25; 304pp On July 12th, 1944, a column of muddy Nazi soldiers in rural Poland flagged down two trucks driven by men wearing German uniforms and asked for a lift. They sat on cylinders in the back, smoking, drying out and cursing the weather. After about half an hour they jumped off, one of them quipping to their new friends: “You carry air!” As Guy Walters observes in his moving and suspenseful book, it was “one of those moments that history would call improbable if the documents [to prove it] did not exist”. The drivers were members of Poland’s resistance movement in disguise, transporting a cargo that could have meant instant death if their passengers had taken a closer look. Those cylinders contained the stolen components of a V-2 rocket, the world’s first long-range ballistic missile and potentially the key to a Nazi victory. “My Wunderwaffe [wonder weapon] will have a decisive effect on the war,” Adolf Hitler boasted to his generals. “The enemy will have no defence against it.” Almost 50ft tall, the V-2 could be blasted to the edge of space before silently descending to Earth at supersonic speed and killing civilians with precisely zero warning. Worried that Hitler was right, British scientists desperately wanted to examine a live specimen for potential weaknesses. When intelligence reports came through that a test V-2 had crashed almost intact into a remote Polish marsh, they saw their chance. A frantic race ensued, with pilots, partisans and politicians all playing crucial roles in what sometimes reads like an old-school war comic. READ MORE Octomum by Patrick Eades: third in The Moth Short Story Prize 2026 The Plot Against Ireland by Myles Dungan: Clear-headed work on a fascinating era Tomorrow by Ava Sedgwick: second in The Moth Short Story Prize 2026 Never Say War. Life inside Russia: Lifting the lid Walters does a highly efficient job of reconstructing this surprisingly little-known episode from every side’s perspective, bolstered by his own emotional visits to the places where it happened. Wisely, he focuses less on technological details and more on complex personalities such as Nazi engineer Wernher von Braun, who later pioneered the US moon landings. [ No one sent up Nazi rocket scientist Wernher von Braun better than satirist Tom Lehrer Opens in new window ] “Science… is like a knife,” he protested when asked about his sinister past. “If you give it to a surgeon or a murderer, each will use it differently.” Walters, also the author of several second World War thrillers, occasionally goes a little too far by inventing dialogue or imagining people’s thought processes. This reservation aside, Stealing Hitler’s Rocket is a thoroughly engaging story of everyday heroism – and practically crying out to be filmed. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Newlyweds Tetiana and Oleksandr celebrate in Kramatorsk. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian ‘At a time when Russia is trying to spread gloom and darkness … it is important to create something beautiful,’ says combat medic Tetiana as she weds army captain Oleksandr By Dan Sabbagh in Kramatorsk. Photographs by Julia Kochetova Sat 29 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n the bright early afternoon sun of Kramatorsk’s central and now ironically named Peace Square, Tetiana, in her bridal dress, and Oleksandr, in his military uniform, are holding up their phones at the ready. It is a public holiday, 35 years since Ukraine’s declaration of independence, and a popular day for a wedding, though the open-air location is not obviously ideal. Three days earlier, Kramatorsk, perhaps Vladimir Putin’s principal target, was formally designated part of the combat zone, the front inching towards the city as Russia closes in on the parts of the Donetsk region it does not control. It is quiet at 2pm though; the ceremony brief. There are no guests other than the Guardian team. View image in fullscreen Tetiana and Oleksandr pose for a wedding photo on Mount Karachun, near Sloviansk, the scene of fierce fighting in 2014. Getting married in Kramatorsk, Oleksandr says, is a necessary act of memory, because soon there may not be much more left to survive. “In this war, all this can just be vaporised, in a few months, in a few days,” the groom explains after the ceremony. “On the battlefield, many cities, towns, small villages where I was two, three years ago, they are now just ruins, just destroyed.” Map showing location of Kramatorsk in Ukraine and in relation to frontline of war A year ago, Kramatorsk was a functioning city, a regional industrial centre, swollen with the presence of the military. It was possible to slowly sip coffee in the street and talk to local people and soldiers about how the city is an intrinsic part of Ukraine. Now it is covered in anti-drone netting, people and businesses are in short supply; many buildings have been bombed, chipboard replacing windows in those still standing. View image in fullscreen En route to Kramatorsk. The truck ahead is carrying ‘dragon’s teeth’, concrete anti-tank obstacles used in fortifications. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Final preparations for the wedding ceremony in Kramatorsk. Six people were reported killed between Saturday and Tuesday in 51 shelling incidents as the city heads towards becoming uninhabitable for all but the most stubborn civilians. Reports swirl that Russia’s elite Rubicon drone unit has deployed to attack a city that Putin wants captured by the end of the year, though his forces will almost certainly take far longer, smashing it as they try to do so. The day before the wedding, Russian quadcopter drones had repeatedly tried to target the vast Ukrainian flag atop an 80-metre (262ft) pole in the city’s central park, just under a mile to the south. There were at least 10 attempts, such is the pettiness of the war at times, and a small tear was visible in the standard afterwards. Yet the couple were determined to marry there, regardless of the threat. View image in fullscreen Tetiana and Oleksandr cross a street beneath anti-drone netting in Kramatorsk. Tetiana says it is “about preserving memories of the Donetsk region, if only in this way”. Oleksandr is from Mariupol, captured after a bloody siege at the beginning of the war , while Tetiana spent “every summer” at her grandmother’s home, now in occupied Donetsk, until she was 15. On her right forearm is a bucolic tattoo, the dacha taking pride of place, its blue tones signifying the Ukrainian region split by over a decade of conflict. A volunteer combat medic – “I don’t want to say no to military service, the number of wounded isn’t getting any smaller”, she says – Tetiana had been based in Kramatorsk until a few days earlier, but her Hospitallers crew was redeployed to Kyiv. Undeterred, she travelled back east the day before to meet Oleksandr, a battle captain on deployment. On the day itself, the pair drove for several more hours, the final miles beneath anti-drone netting, to reach their chosen wedding location on time. U kraine introduced online weddings in 2024, a necessity in a war in which soldiers and their partners can be physically separated for months on end. The service has rapidly gained popularity in a digitally literate country – 38% of marriages were conducted online in the first half of the year, according to Ukraine’s justice ministry. Though Tetiana and Oleksandr were together, the officiant was on a video call. The two met as recently as February, after she had reached out online, offering to treat him. Each already looks sure of the other. Oleksandr believes their shared understanding of the war, forced on to their country, will bind them close, at a time when “there is a big gap between military and civilians”. Her “experience in battlefield medical evacuations and so on makes it easier for us to understand each other,” he says. View image in fullscreen Tetiana and Oleksandr pose for a photo outside a railway station in Kramatorsk, where trains have not stopped since early November 2025 because of security concerns. Their adult lives have been dominated by the conflict. Tetiana and Oleksandr are the same age as Ukraine itself – 35 – meaning they would have been in their early 20s when Russian-backed separatists captured Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk in April 2014, beginning fighting in eastern Ukraine that has never ended. Both cities were liberated that July, and only now has the frontline returned. Proceedings begin promptly. Bride and groom hold their phones forward; the town’s already battered Palace of Culture, a five-storey museum and landmark in the Soviet classical style, behind. They place a white, traditional embroidered cloth, a rushnyk , in front of them, though it will not stay down in the wind. View image in fullscreen Oleksandr carries loose tiles to hold the rushnyk in place for the ceremony. Oleksandr brings over two loose tiles, taken from the square’s flooring, to hold the rushnyk in place. The newlyweds will take the tiles with them afterwards. It is not an act of vandalism but rather one of preservation, taking tiles from a square that was relaid six years ago as part of the decommunisation of what had been Lenin Square. Tetiana plans to break the tiles and make a mosaic with them. View image in fullscreen Tetiana and Oleksandr before the ceremony. The empty central square is surrounded by ‘dragon’s teeth’ and anti-drone netting. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Tetiana and Oleksandr step on to the wedding rushnyk, a traditional embroidered cloth. The ritual symbolises the start of the couple’s life together. Rings and vows are exchanged, a bridal kiss is shared, and the couple step on the rushnyk together. This is an act of egalitarianism; tradition holds that whoever steps on the embroidered towel first has the last word in the family. After a few more photographs, it is time to head indoors to the nearby Sweet Coffee House Bakery, one of the few businesses still open, though its owner, Kateryna Seledtsova, has relocated to Kharkiv and the cafe feels more like a shelter, albeit one with cream cakes inside. View image in fullscreen There is a moment of worry in the cafe, because a drone has been spotted above while Tetiana is outside. But she is quickly found and, over wedding cake, the newlyweds focus on their plans for children. “Starting a family during the war is about hope. I think it’s important to build something new, to build something beautiful, in a world that Russia is trying to destroy,” she says. View image in fullscreen The newlyweds in Sweet Coffee House Bakery, one of the few businesses still open. “I think that at a time when Russia is trying to spread gloom and darkness, destroy us and frighten us, it is important to create something beautiful, to wear beautiful clothes, to do kind deeds, to help and look after one another, and to love one another. That is what Russia wants to take away from us.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Marriage Family Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money

Robot valet parking at Gatwick Airport promises safer, easier long‑stay car storage Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 15/09/2026 - 13:16 GMT+2 London Gatwick Airport is testing car-parking robots, offering secure, automated long-stay parking for most vehicles at a small extra cost. … More The robots, developed by French company Stanley Robotics , can park cars with centimetre-level precision. Gatwick says the system can accommodate around 95% of vehicles , although some cars are excluded. Vehicles must weigh no more than 2.6 tonnes , be under 2.3 metres tall, have a wheelbase of less than 3.3 metres and wheels no larger than 21 inches (53,34 centimètres) . ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The parking area is protected by perimeter fencing, floodlighting and 24-hour security patrols, while automatic number plate recognition monitors vehicles entering and leaving the site. Stanley Robotics says the robots are designed to stop if they malfunction, rather than move unpredictably. Some passengers say the service is quick and easy to book, while others have opted for it because of the added security. The service costs around €6 to €12 more (£5 to £10) than standard long-stay parking. When it launched, the service required a minimum stay of five days and was mainly available on weekdays between 9 am and 5 pm . Gatwick says these restrictions will be gradually eased. https://www.portfolio.hu/global/20261114.text: Az Egyesült Államok legnagyobb és legészakibb államának számító Alaszka közismert arról, hogy a végtelen fagyos területek alatt hatalmas ásványkincs-készletek lapulnak. A tundra alatt rejtőző, kiaknázatlan földgáz felkutatására az Egyesült Arab Emírségek egyik vállalata jelezte érdeklődését, ez pedig nyitott fülekre talált Washingtonban is. Az ígéretek között szerepelt, hogy egy bizonyos időt követően a létesítmény majd amerikai tulajdonba kerül, a döntéshozók pedig remek energetikai lehetőséget láttak az elképzelésben. Úgy vélték, hogy a kitermelt mennyiség hozzájárulhat a térség gazdasági fellendüléséhez az exporton keresztül. A projekthez megérkeztek az első felmérők, a tengerfenéken végeztek kutatásokat, méghozzá a Transzalaszka Csővezeték-rendszer közvetlen közelében. Ez egyébként az amerikai energia-ellátás egyik kulcsfontosságú eleme. A közelben az amerikai katonai alakulatok több tagja végzett műveleteket, például a tengeralattjárók gyakorolták a befagyott tengeren a merülést és a felszínre emelkedést. A vizsgálatok ugyanakkor egyáltalán nem voltak nemzetbiztonsági szempontból ártatlanok, ugyanis rengeteg adat jutott el innen az orosz Novatekhez, mivel valójában innen irányították a projektet. Az egyelőre nem világos, hogy pontosan milyen mélységben és milyen részletességgel gyűjtöttek adatokat Alaszka nemzetbiztonsági szempontból rendkívül érzékeny térségéből. Heather Conley, a Külügyminisztérium korábbi tisztviselője elmondta, hogy ez „szuperérzékenynek számító terület”: Bármilyen tudományos adat azonnal kettős felhasználású, ami azt jelenti, hogy mind katonai, mind polgári célokat szolgálhat Az elmúlt években egyértelműen növekedett az oroszok fenyegető jelenléte az északi sarkvidéken, erről már a norvég biztonsági szolgálatok is beszámoltak. Troy Bouffard, a fairbanksi Alaszkai Egyetem Sarkvidéki Biztonsági és Rugalmassági Központjának igazgatója egyenesen hírszerzési kudarcnak nevezte, hogy egy orosz vállalat ilyen térségben végezhetett felméréseket. Az információszerzés egészen 2026 őszéig zajlott, eddigre viszont többen is felhívták a figyelmet, hogy valójában egy orosz „cselről” van szó. A helyi leányvállalat, a Polar Train vezérigazgatója, Joel Riddle és stábja arra sürgette a finanszírozókat, hogy keressenek más helyszínt a kutatásokhoz, mivel a kiszemelt térség nem ideális a beruházásokhoz, de ez sem hatotta meg a hivatalosan az Egyesült Arab Emírségekből érkező csapatot. A Novatek kifejezetten elutasította, hogy kényes adatokat igyekeznek szerezni a projekten keresztül az Egyesült Államok stratégiai infrastruktúrájáról. Szerintük arra koncentrálnak, hogy minél gyorsabban beindulhasson a kitermelés és elépüljön az LNG-hez szükséges infrastruktúra. Az ügy politikai témává lett, mivel Donald Trump az elmúlt időszakban az energetikai területen fokozni próbálta az együttműködését Oroszországgal, mindezt felhasználva – hivatalosan – az ukrajnai háború lezárásához. A mostani eset azonban több amerikai törvényhozó számára is problémaként jelent meg, és kezdeményezték, hogy a jövőben a kínai és az orosz járművek e nagyon közlekedhessen az amerikai Arktisz-közeli vizeken. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm87.text: Figure caption, Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack By Claire Keenan Published 19 November 2026, 01:05 GMT Updated 39 minutes ago The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said. The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea. The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water. The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China . Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way. Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv. At least four people were killed in a Russian drone attack on the southern city of Odesa on Wednesday, according to Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives". President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making. Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine Published 1 day ago Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road. That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse. In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before". While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line. Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days. Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.
